title: Ring Router
statement: A cache cluster places servers at integer positions on a ring and sends every request key to the first server found clockwise: the server with the smallest position that is >= the key, wrapping around to the server with the smallest position overall when no server sits at or after the key. Servers can join and leave. The operations are ["add", name, position], which adds a server and returns true, or returns false and changes nothing if that name is already in use or that position already holds a server; ["remove", name], which removes the server and returns true, or returns false if there is no such server; and ["route", key], which returns the name of the server that handles key, or null when the cluster is empty. Apply the operations in order starting from an empty cluster and return the result of every operation.
constraints: Each operation is exactly ["add", name, position], ["remove", name] or ["route", key]

examples.explanation: Key 100 lands exactly on alpha; 101 goes on to beta (500); 501 wraps around to alpha. After beta leaves, 101 wraps to alpha. Position 100 is taken, so adding gamma there fails.
An empty cluster routes to null and has nothing to remove.

hints.content: A route call only depends on the servers' positions in sorted order.
A linear scan can find the smallest position >= key, falling back to the smallest position overall. That costs O(servers) per route.
Keep the positions in a sorted array. Finding the first position >= key is a lower-bound binary search.
If the search runs off the end of the array, wrap around to index 0. Keep a parallel array of names, and a map from name to position so removal can find the right index.
Insert and remove with splice at the index the search returns, so the array stays sorted and positions stay unique. Check for a duplicate name or position before inserting.

testCases.explanation: Joins, exact hits, wrap-around, a removal and a rejected add.
A key at, before and after each server position, including wrap-around.
Duplicate names and positions are rejected; the cluster empties again.
A freed position and a freed name can be reused.
A random workload of adds, removals and routes over 40 possible server names.
300 servers followed by a long stream of routes with occasional removals.

solutions.title: Scan every server
solutions.intuition: Keep the servers in an unsorted list and find the right one by inspecting all of them.
solutions.approach: add checks every server for the same name or position; remove filters the list; route scans all servers for the smallest position >= key and also remembers the smallest position overall for wrap-around.
solutions.pseudocode:
servers = []
add: if any server has the name or position: false else push; true
remove: filter by name
route: best = min position >= key, else min position overall
solutions.timeComplexity: O(s) per operation for s current servers
commonMistakes: Choosing the closest position instead of the first one clockwise.
Forgetting the wrap-around when no position is >= key.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Scanning the whole cluster for every request is simple and obviously right, but every route costs time proportional to the number of servers.

steps.title: Route 101
steps.content: With servers at 100 and 500, scanning finds 500 as the smallest position >= 101.

steps.title: Route 501
steps.content: No position is >= 501, so the smallest position overall (100, alpha) is used.

solutions.title: Sorted positions with a lower-bound search
solutions.intuition: The ring is a sorted list read circularly, so the handler is the first position at or after the key, found by binary search.
solutions.approach: Maintain a sorted array of positions with a parallel array of names and a name-to-position map. lowerBound(target) returns the first index with position >= target. route wraps to index 0 when that index equals the length. add and remove locate the index by lowerBound and splice.
solutions.pseudocode:
route(key): if empty: null; i = lowerBound(key); return names[i == len ? 0 : i]
add(name, pos): i = lowerBound(pos); reject if name known or positions[i] == pos; splice in
remove(name): i = lowerBound(where[name]); splice out
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log s) per route; O(s) per successful add or remove because splice shifts the array, plus an O(log s) search
commonMistakes: Using the index returned by the search without handling the case where it equals the array length.
Forgetting to update the name-to-position map on removal.
Treating route as O(1) or add as O(log s): splicing a plain array shifts elements.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This is consistent hashing reduced to its data structure. The positions sit in a sorted array, so the owner of a key is a lower-bound lookup with a wrap-around. Routing is O(log s). Membership changes are rare in practice, and with a plain array they cost O(s) because splice shifts elements; a balanced tree or skip list would make every operation O(log s). In real systems each server also gets many virtual positions so load spreads evenly and a departing server hands its keys to several neighbours rather than one.

steps.title: Build the ring
steps.content: After the two adds, positions = [100, 500] and names = [alpha, beta].

steps.title: Look up keys
steps.content: lowerBound(101) = 1 (beta); lowerBound(501) = 2 = length, so wrap to index 0 (alpha).

steps.title: Membership change
steps.content: Removing beta splices index 1 out. Position 100 stays taken, so adding gamma there returns false.
